lead: Any periodic signal, however awkward its shape, is a sum of sinusoids at the fundamental frequency and its multiples. Orthogonality lets you pull out each sinusoid's share with one integral over one period. That share is the Fourier coefficient. Engineers use this to read a waveform's spectrum, predict what a filter outputs for a periodic input, and describe the harmonic currents a rectifier or fan regulator pushes into the mains. This chapter builds both forms and lists the properties that make them quick to apply.
prereq: You need: periodic signals, even and odd symmetry, and orthogonal signals (see the topics Classification: energy, power, periodic, even and odd signals and Signals as vectors: orthogonal signal space).

blocks.text: A signal is periodic when x(t) = x(t + T₀) for every t, where T₀ is the smallest positive value that works: the period, in seconds. The fundamental frequency f₀ = 1/T₀ is in hertz. The fundamental angular frequency ω₀ = 2π/T₀ is in radians per second. The n-th harmonic is the sinusoid at n f₀ hertz, or nω₀ rad/s, for n = 1, 2, 3, …
Fourier's claim is that x(t) equals a sum of these harmonics. Write ∫<sub>T₀</sub> … dt for an integral over any interval of length T₀. Products of harmonics behave like this:
∫T₀ cos(nω₀t)cos(mω₀t)dt = T₀/2 if n = m ≥ 1, T₀ if n = m = 0, and 0 if n ≠ m
Here n and m are harmonic numbers; ω₀ = 2π/T₀ rad/s; the integral runs over one period of T₀ seconds. The same holds for sines, and ∫<sub>T₀</sub> sin(nω₀t)cos(mω₀t)dt = 0 for all n and m.

This is orthogonality: different harmonics do not overlap. Multiply x(t) by cos(nω₀t) and integrate over a period; every harmonic except the n-th averages to zero, and the n-th survives with a factor T₀/2. Each coefficient needs one integral, not a search.

sections.h3: Two forms of the same series

blocks.text: Here x(t) is the periodic signal with period T₀ seconds; ω₀ = 2π/T₀ rad/s; aₙ and bₙ are real coefficients in the units of x(t); a₀/2 is the average or DC value.
Here the factor 2/T₀ cancels the T₀/2 from orthogonality; all three integrals run over one period. Every non-zero aₙ or bₙ shows a sinusoid actually present in x(t).
Here cₙ is complex in general and has the units of x(t); the sum runs over negative as well as positive n; e<sup>jnω₀t</sup> = cos(nω₀t) + j sin(nω₀t). This is the exponential form.
c₀ = a₀/2, cₙ = (aₙ − jbₙ)/2, c−n = cₙ* for real x(t)

Here the star means complex conjugate; aₙ and bₙ are the trigonometric coefficients. For real x(t), |cₙ| = ½√(aₙ² + bₙ²), so a cosine of amplitude Aₙ = √(aₙ² + bₙ²) appears as two lines of height Aₙ/2 at +nω₀ and −nω₀.

The exponential form is compact: one integral, one symbol, and a time shift or derivative becomes a plain multiplication. The trigonometric form speaks in real cosines and sines, which is what a spectrum display shows on its positive-frequency side. Dirichlet conditions: if x(t) is absolutely integrable over one period, with finitely many maxima, minima and discontinuities there, the series converges to x(t) at each point of continuity and to the midpoint of a jump at a discontinuity. Near a jump the partial sums ring, overshooting by about 9% of the jump height; adding terms narrows the ringing but never removes that overshoot. This is the Gibbs phenomenon.
Write cₙ for x(t) and dₙ for a second signal y(t) with the same period.

Linearity needs a common period; if the periods differ, use the least common multiple. Time scaling by a > 0 squeezes the period to T₀/a seconds and moves each harmonic to n(aω₀) rad/s, while every cₙ keeps its value. Integration requires zero mean: only when c₀ = 0 is ∫x(t)dt periodic, and then its coefficient is cₙ/(jnω₀) for n ≠ 0, while the n = 0 term is an arbitrary constant. If c₀ ≠ 0 the integral contains a ramp and is not periodic. A time shift leaves |cₙ| unchanged and adds phase −nω₀t₀; a general linear filter multiplies each cₙ by H(jnω₀), changing both magnitude and phase.

Symmetry saves arithmetic. A real even signal has every bₙ = 0 and real, even cₙ: a cosine-only series. A real odd signal has every aₙ = 0, hence a₀ = 0, and purely imaginary, odd cₙ: a sine-only series. Half-wave symmetry, x(t ± T₀/2) = −x(t), kills the DC term and all even harmonics, leaving n = 1, 3, 5, …. The square-wave current drawn from a 50 Hz supply by a bridge rectifier with a large inductive load behaves this way: its harmonics sit at 50, 150, 250 Hz, and the even ones are absent.

figure.caption: The pulse of the worked example (top) and its two-sided line spectrum (bottom). Every even harmonic is zero, and the lines follow the dashed sinc-shaped envelope; a line below the axis means a cosine term with a minus sign.

examples.question: The periodic pulse x(t) = 1 for −1 < t < 1 s and x(t) = 0 for 1 < |t| < 2 s repeats with period T₀ = 4 s. Find c₀ and the general cₙ, then write the exponential Fourier series and the trigonometric Fourier series with the first three non-zero cosine terms.
steps: Period T₀ = 4 s, so ω₀ = 2π/T₀ = 2π/4 = π/2 rad/s ≈ 1.5708 rad/s.
DC term: c₀ = (1/T₀)∫<sub>T₀</sub>x(t)dt = (1/4)∫<sub>−1</sub><sup>1</sup>1 dt = (1/4)(2 s) = 0.5. The pulse is high for 2 s of every 4 s, so the average is 0.5.
Divide by T₀ = 4: cₙ = sin(nπ/2)/(nπ) for n ≠ 0.

Numbers: c₁ = sin(π/2)/π = 1/π ≈ 0.3183; c₂ = sin(π)/(2π) = 0; c₃ = sin(3π/2)/(3π) = −1/(3π) ≈ −0.1061; c₅ = 1/(5π) ≈ 0.0637. Even n give zero because the pulse is centered and high for exactly half the period, so sin(nπ/2) = 0 for even n.
Exponential series: x(t) = 0.5 + Σ<sub>n≠0</sub> [sin(nπ/2)/(nπ)]e<sup>jn(π/2)t</sup>, with n running over ±1, ±3, ±5, …
x(t) is real and even, so bₙ = 0 and aₙ = 2cₙ = 2 sin(nπ/2)/(nπ): a₁ = 0.6366, a₃ = −0.2122.
examples.answer: c₀ = 0.5 and cₙ = sin(nπ/2)/(nπ) for n ≠ 0, giving x(t) = 0.5 + Σ<sub>n≠0</sub>[sin(nπ/2)/(nπ)]e<sup>jn(π/2)t</sup> = 0.5 + (2/π)cos(πt/2) − (2/(3π))cos(3πt/2) + (2/(5π))cos(5πt/2) − …, with cosine amplitudes 0.6366, 0.2122 and 0.1273.
examples.check:
import math
def cn(n):
    return 0.5 if n == 0 else math.sin(n*math.pi/2)/(n*math.pi)
print(round(cn(0), 4))
print(round(cn(1), 4))
print(round(cn(2), 4))
print(round(cn(3), 4))
print(round(2*cn(1), 4))

traps: Dropping the 1/T₀ in front of the cₙ integral, or using 2/T₀ for cₙ because the trigonometric form uses 2/T₀ for aₙ. Dropping 1/T₀ multiplies every cₙ by T₀; using 2/T₀ instead of 1/T₀ doubles every cₙ.
Writing ω₀ = 1/T₀. The fundamental frequency is f₀ = 1/T₀ hertz, but the angular frequency is ω₀ = 2π/T₀ rad/s, and every harmonic multiple must use ω₀.

Mixing the two DC conventions. With x(t) = a₀/2 + Σ… and a₀ = (2/T₀)∫x(t)dt, as in this book, the DC value is a₀/2 = c₀. Some books write x(t) = a₀ + Σ… with a₀ = (1/T₀)∫x(t)dt, and then a₀ itself is the DC value. Pick one convention and keep it through the answer.
Summing the exponential series only from n = 1. The sum runs from −∞ to ∞, and for real signals c<sub>−n</sub> = cₙ*, so the cosine amplitude is 2|cₙ|, not |cₙ|.
Getting the sign wrong in a time shift: x(t − t₀) multiplies cₙ by e<sup>−jnω₀t₀</sup>. A delay gives a negative phase; e<sup>+jnω₀t₀</sup> is a time advance.

quiz.q: Define the period, fundamental frequency and fundamental angular frequency of a periodic signal.
quiz.a: Period T₀: the smallest positive value with x(t) = x(t + T₀), in seconds. Frequency f₀ = 1/T₀ hertz. Angular frequency ω₀ = 2π/T₀ rad/s. The n-th harmonic is at n f₀ or nω₀.

quiz.q: State the Dirichlet conditions and the Gibbs phenomenon in one line each.
quiz.a: Absolute integrability over one period plus finitely many maxima, minima and discontinuities there makes the series converge, to the midpoint of a jump at the jump. Gibbs: near a discontinuity the partial sum overshoots by about 9% of the jump height.

quiz.q: For a real signal, what is the relation between cₙ and c<sub>−n</sub>, and what does that say about the magnitude spectrum?
quiz.a: c<sub>−n</sub> = cₙ*, a complex conjugate, because the signal has no imaginary part. Hence |c<sub>−n</sub>| = |cₙ|: the two-sided magnitude spectrum is even, and each cosine of amplitude Aₙ appears as two lines of height Aₙ/2.

quiz.q: A periodic signal with T₀ = 2 s has c₁ = 0.3 − j0.4. Find a₁, b₁ and the amplitude of the first cosine term.
quiz.a: a₁ − jb₁ = 2c₁ = 0.6 − j0.8, so a₁ = 0.6 and b₁ = 0.8. Amplitude A₁ = √(0.6² + 0.8²) = 1.0, equal to 2|c₁| = 2(0.5) = 1.0.

quiz.q: c₁ of x(t) is 2 + j0, with T₀ = 4 s. Find c₁ of x(t − 0.5).
quiz.a: ω₀ = 2π/4 = π/2 rad/s. c₁ becomes c₁e<sup>−j(π/2)(0.5)</sup> = 2e<sup>−jπ/4</sup> = 2(0.7071 − j0.7071) = 1.4142 − j1.4142. Magnitude stays 2; only phase changed.

quiz.q: An even periodic signal also satisfies x(t − T₀/2) = −x(t). Which coefficients vanish and why?
quiz.a: Even symmetry forces bₙ = 0. Half-wave symmetry forces cₙ = 0 for even n and c₀ = 0, since shifting by half a period multiplies cₙ by e<sup>−jnπ</sup> = (−1)ⁿ, which must equal −1. Only odd n survive, with a cosine-only series.

beyond: Not for the exam. The fast Fourier transform evaluates N coefficients in about N log₂N operations instead of N²; spectrum analysers and vibration monitors use it directly. The two-sided exponential form is also the everyday language of OFDM radios, which work with complex baseband signals.
